subject: giant mice island
title: What If Mice Grew Big Enough to Attack Albatrosses? On One Island They Did

scenes.text: What if house mice grew big enough to attack an albatross? On one island, they did.
Gough Island, in the South Atlantic, holds 22 seabird species. Mice arrived on ships in the 1800s and found no predators.
Over generations they grew to twice the size of mainland mice. And they learned a chick on a nest doesn't move.
Scientists estimate the mice kill about 1.7 million chicks a year, including the Tristan albatross, down to 199 breeding pairs.
In 2021, helicopters dropped poison bait across the island. By December, a single mouse appeared on a camera. The operation had failed.
Yet in 2022, chicks fledged from 1,186 of 1,570 nests, far more than before. The mice are back. The clock is running again.

description:
What if mice grew large enough to prey on albatrosses? On Gough Island in the South Atlantic, house mice introduced in the 19th century have grown to twice the size of mainland mice and attack seabird chicks on their nests.
Researchers estimated the mice kill about 1.7 million chicks a year, threatening the critically endangered Tristan albatross, which has only 199 breeding pairs there. A 2021 eradication attempt by the RSPB and the Tristan da Cunha government dropped bait by helicopter, but a mouse was filmed that December. Breeding success still jumped in 2022.
What should we run through next?
first_comment: Rodents have been removed from more than 700 islands worldwide, so the plan can work; Gough is just the hardest case yet. Which island invasion should we run through next?
